gloss_terse: alabaster jar; a small, handleless perfume flask typically carved from alabaster stone
gloss_readable: In the ancient Mediterranean world, perfumes and precious ointments were stored in small globular flasks carved from alabaster, a translucent mineral prized for preserving fragrance. The Greek term refers not to the stone itself but to the vessel made from it. All four New Testament occurrences describe a woman breaking open such a jar to anoint Jesus (Matt 26:7; Mark 14:3; Luke 7:37), an act of costly devotion since the sealed neck had to be snapped to release the contents.

senses.1: A small, handleless perfume vessel typically carved from alabaster stone, designed with a sealed neck to preserve costly ointments. The multilingual evidence consistently renders this as a container rather than the mineral: Spanish 'frasco de alabastro' (flask of alabaster) and French 'vase d'albatre' both emphasize the vessel. Every NT use involves anointing Jesus with expensive nard or perfume.

gloss_terse: Hallelujah; a Hebrew liturgical exclamation meaning 'Praise the LORD'
gloss_readable: This untranslated Hebrew exclamation combines hallel ('praise') with Yah (the shortened form of YHWH), literally meaning 'Praise the LORD!' It appears exclusively in Revelation 19:1-6, where the heavenly multitude erupts in fourfold praise after Babylon's fall. No other New Testament book uses it, making it a deliberate echo of the Psalter's Hallel psalms (Pss 113-118, 146-150) now resounding in the eschatological throne room.

senses.1: A transliterated Hebrew liturgical shout meaning 'Praise Yah(weh)!', preserved untranslated across all target languages—English 'Hallelouia,' Spanish 'Halleluia,' French and German 'Halleluja'—reflecting its status as a universal worship cry. Confined to the four occurrences in Revelation 19:1-6, it marks the climactic heavenly celebration of God's righteous judgment.

gloss_terse: sinful act; a concrete deed of wrongdoing or moral failure
gloss_readable: Where the more common hamartia (G0266) denotes sin as a condition or principle, this noun emphasizes the individual sinful act—a particular deed that misses the mark. Aristotle placed it midway between deliberate injustice and mere misfortune. In Mark 3:28-29 Jesus distinguishes forgivable sins from the unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit; in Romans 3:25 Paul speaks of God passing over former sins; and in 1 Corinthians 6:18 the term highlights that sexual immorality is a sin committed against one's own body.

senses.1: A concrete sinful deed or moral failure, distinguished from the abstract principle of sin (hamartia). Spanish 'pecado' and French 'peche' mirror the singular/plural pattern visible in the Greek occurrences. Mark 3:28-29 pairs it with 'blasphemies' to enumerate forgivable offenses; Romans 3:25 uses it for past transgressions God overlooked; 1 Corinthians 6:18 specifies a sin enacted against one's own body.

gloss_terse: to neglect, disregard; to fail to give proper care or attention to something important
gloss_readable: Derived from the adjective ameles ('careless'), this verb describes a willful or culpable failure to attend to what matters. Its semantic range moves from casual indifference to serious spiritual negligence. In Matthew 22:5 the invited guests simply 'paid no attention' to the king's banquet invitation, while Hebrews 2:3 raises the stakes dramatically: 'How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?' The verb thus spans everyday carelessness and eternally consequential disregard.

senses.1: To be negligent or careless toward something deserving attention, ranging from casual indifference to culpable spiritual disregard. Spanish 'descuidar' (to be careless) and French 'negliger' both capture the willful inattention. Matthew 22:5 depicts guests ignoring a royal wedding invitation; 1 Timothy 4:14 warns Timothy not to neglect his spiritual gift; Hebrews 2:3 escalates to neglecting salvation itself; Hebrews 8:9 recalls God's turning away from Israel who disregarded his covenant.

gloss_terse: undefiled, pure; free from moral or ritual contamination
gloss_readable: Formed with the alpha-privative prefix on miaino ('to stain, defile'), this adjective describes what remains utterly free from contamination—whether moral, ritual, or physical. In Hebrews 7:26, Christ as high priest is 'holy, innocent, undefiled'; in Hebrews 13:4 it characterizes the marriage bed that must be kept pure. James 1:27 applies it to genuine religion 'undefiled before God,' and 1 Peter 1:4 describes the believer's heavenly inheritance as imperishable and undefiled.

senses.1: Free from any stain, defilement, or moral contamination—pure in the fullest sense. Both German and French render it 'unbefleckt' and the concept aligns closely, while Spanish distinguishes 'incontaminada' (uncontaminated) from 'sin mancha' (without blemish), hinting at both ritual and moral dimensions. Applied to Christ's priestly character (Heb 7:26), marital fidelity (Heb 13:4), pure religion (Jas 1:27), and the heavenly inheritance (1 Pet 1:4).

gloss_terse: lamb; used in the NT exclusively as a christological title for Jesus
gloss_readable: Though the common Greek word for a young sheep, every New Testament occurrence carries unmistakable sacrificial and messianic weight. John the Baptist twice identifies Jesus as 'the Lamb of God' (John 1:29, 36), echoing both the Passover lamb and Isaiah's suffering servant. Acts 8:32 quotes Isaiah 53:7 directly—'as a lamb before its shearer is silent'—and 1 Peter 1:19 speaks of redemption through 'the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish.' The consistent christological focus sets this term apart from arnion, the diminutive 'lamb' of Revelation.

senses.1: A lamb viewed as a sacrificial or christological figure, not merely a young sheep. Spanish distinguishes capitalized 'Cordero' (the Lamb, christological) from lowercase 'cordero' (generic lamb), a distinction visible across the four occurrences. French 'agneau' (cognate with Latin agnus, itself likely related to the Greek amnos) preserves the same dual register. All NT uses point to Jesus as the fulfillment of Passover and Isaianic sacrifice imagery (John 1:29, 36; Acts 8:32; 1 Pet 1:19).

gloss_terse: to clothe, dress; to put garments on someone
gloss_readable: An older, somewhat literary verb for dressing or clothing someone, used in the NT exclusively by Jesus in two parallel sayings about God's providential care. In Matthew 6:30 and Luke 12:28, Jesus argues from lesser to greater: if God so clothes the grass of the field, how much more will he clothe his followers? Matthew 11:8 and Luke 7:25 use the perfect passive participle to describe someone 'dressed in' fine garments, contrasting John the Baptist's rough attire with courtly luxury.

senses.1: To put clothing on someone, to dress or array a person or thing in garments. French 'vetir' and Spanish 'vestir' both derive from Latin vestire, capturing the same basic action. The active forms in Matt 6:30 and Luke 12:28 describe God clothing the grass with splendor; the passive participle in Matt 11:8 and Luke 7:25 depicts a person dressed in luxurious garments, contrasting with the ascetic simplicity of the Baptist.

gloss_terse: to bind under a curse; to invoke divine destruction on oneself if an oath is broken
gloss_readable: This verb intensifies ordinary oath-taking by invoking anathema—a solemn self-curse calling down divine punishment if the vow is violated. In Mark 14:71, Peter's denial reaches its climax as he begins 'to curse and swear,' placing himself under the ban. The three Acts passages (23:12, 14, 21) describe a conspiracy of more than forty men who 'bound themselves under a curse' not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul—a dramatic narrative detail showing the lethal seriousness of such oaths in Second Temple Judaism.

senses.1: To place oneself or others under a solemn curse (anathema), invoking divine punishment for oath-breaking. Spanish 'maldecir/maldijimos' (to curse) and French 'prononcer un anatheme' (to pronounce an anathema) highlight the self-imprecatory nature. Mark 14:71 describes Peter cursing himself during his denial; Acts 23:12-21 recounts conspirators who bound themselves under a curse—a religiously binding vow to assassinate Paul or face divine retribution.

gloss_terse: to return, turn back; to bend one's path back to a previous location
gloss_readable: Compounded from ana ('back') and kampto ('to bend'), this verb pictures a path curving back on itself. The Magi return home by another route to avoid Herod (Matt 2:12). In Luke 10:6, Jesus instructs the seventy-two that if a household is unworthy, their peace 'will return' to them—a striking image of blessing boomeranging back. Paul promises the Ephesian elders he will return (Acts 18:21), and the heroes of faith in Hebrews 11:15 are praised for not longing to return to the country they had left.

senses.1: To turn back or return to a place previously departed from, literally bending one's course in reverse. Spanish 'volver/regresar' and French 'retourner' capture the straightforward spatial meaning. Matt 2:12 has the Magi returning by another road; Luke 10:6 metaphorically pictures peace returning to the sender; Acts 18:21 records Paul's promise to come back; Hebrews 11:15 notes the patriarchs' refusal to return to their homeland.

gloss_terse: to straighten up, stand erect; to lift one's head or body from a bent posture
gloss_readable: Formed from ana ('up') and kupto ('to bend, stoop'), this verb describes the physical motion of raising oneself from a stooped or bowed position. In Luke 13:11, the woman crippled for eighteen years was unable to 'straighten up at all' until Jesus healed her. Luke 21:28 uses it eschatologically: 'Stand up and lift your heads, for your redemption draws near.' In John 8:7 and 8:10, Jesus straightens up from writing on the ground to address the woman's accusers—a quiet, powerful gesture of deliberate attention.

senses.1: To raise oneself from a bent or stooped posture, to stand erect or lift the head. Spanish 'enderezarse' (to straighten oneself) and French 'se relever' (to raise oneself up) both emphasize the reflexive, embodied nature of the action. Luke 13:11 describes a woman physically unable to straighten up; Luke 21:28 uses it figuratively for confident expectation; John 8:7, 10 depict Jesus rising from stooping to write on the ground.
